motivation: The current academic peer review system is a critical component of scientific advancement and quality control, yet it is often time-consuming, biased, and arbitrary. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a new system that incorporates large language models (LLMs) to assist in the peer review process, aiming to enhance its efficiency and quality. Existing methods, such as blind and open review systems, have their strengths and weaknesses, but they struggle to balance the subjectivity of research expertise, the effort required from reviewers, and the alignment between reviewers' opinions with overall ratings. The significance of this research lies in improving the review system to advance AI, data science, and information science, which have been identified as key areas for growth by the Artificial Intelligence Index. The paper's approach focuses on creating a review system that leverages LLMs to assist reviewers and provide community-wide guidance, thereby reducing bias and improving the overall quality of the peer review process.
idea: The paper introduces a pilot review system that incorporates large language models (LLMs) to assist in the peer review process of academic conferences. The proposed system, which includes Author-Assisted Evaluation (Author-AAE) and Community-Guided Review (CGR), aims to address the limitations of existing review methods by reducing subjectivity and enhancing the quality of reviews. The system allows authors to provide their own scores for their work, which are considered by LLM-based reviewers, and it also incorporates community feedback to refine the reviews. The results suggest that this approach improves the fairness and efficiency of the peer review process, with LLM-based reviews scoring highly in both 'Reproducibility and Quality' and 'Review Quality'.
title: A Pilot Study Evaluating Large Language Models as Reviewers at Academic Conferences
abstract:
This paper presents a new system for academic peer review that is more objective, efficient, and community-guided. Our system incorporates \emph{author-assisted evaluation} (Author-AAE) and \emph{community-guided review} (CGR) into the peer review of AI conferences. This is in contrast to existing approaches that prioritize alternative systems that only address some of these challenges. Our evaluation uses data from three major AI conferences that used our system and from a survey of reviewers. Their feedback indicates that our system's reviews are superior to single-LLM-based reviews due to their reduced subjectivity and enhanced quality. The reviewers' scores for our system's reviews were significantly higher than for single-LLM-based reviews across multiple metrics: ``Reproducibility and Quality'' (by 0.427 $\pm$ 0.007), ``Review Quality'' (by 0.265 $\pm$ 0.09), and ``Alignment between opinion and paper score'' (by 0.503 $\pm$ 0.090). 
In addition, we discovered that single-LLM-based reviews are more likely to be rejected by the program committee after author major revisions (on average by 0.182 $\pm$ 0.103) and are much more likely to be rejected overall (on average by 0.300 $\pm$ 0.124), compared to our system's reviews. These results suggest that our system performs better in reducing the arbitrary nature of the current peer review system and can serve as an inspiration for the scientific community to explore new review systems.

Experimental_Setup.name: Acceptance Results Analysis
Experimental_Setup.description: The purpose of this experiment is to measure the acceptance rates of papers under different review systems. The datasets used include papers from Aaai 2024, CoRLL 2024, and the ICML 2023 dataset. The methodology involves conducting a series of Z-tests for all combinations of datasets and reviewers. The reviewer scores are weighted by the importance of the review section for the paper. The results are compared to human reviews and single-LLM-based reviews. The experiment aims to check if the proposed system performs similarly to human reviews in terms of paper acceptance rates, providing evidence that it will not negatively impact the outcomes of the peer review process.

Experimental_Setup.name: Review Quality Analysis with Human Reviewers
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment aims to measure the opinions of reviewers about the quality of reviews provided by the single-LLM-based review process versus the proposed system. A survey is conducted where each reviewer is presented with a paper and a pair of reviews from each system. The reviewers are asked to decide which review is better, even if they are not familiar with the specific style of reviewing. The experiment ensures that both pairs are the same length to facilitate a fair comparison. The reviewers are paid $15 for their participation. The metrics used include REJ (reviewed paper score), ACC (accepted paper score), REJ+ (rejected paper review score), and ACC- (accepted paper review score). The results are compared to check if the proposed system's reviews are perceived as higher quality.

Experimental_Setup.name: Subjectivity Analysis
Experimental_Setup.description: The purpose of this experiment is to measure the subjectivity of the AAE and reviewer scores. The methodology involves analyzing the correlation between owner scores and paper scores across different review settings, such as reviewed paper score (REJ), accepted paper score (ACC), rejected paper review score (REJ+), and accepted paper review score (ACC-). The experiment uses datasets from Aaai 2024 and CoRLL 2024. The analysis aims to identify potential bias in the owner's score and how it correlates with the paper's quality. The results help assess the effectiveness of the proposed system in reducing subjectivity and ensuring fairer reviews.

Experimental_Setup.name: Rebuttal Alignment Analysis
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment measures the alignment of reviews with author opinions during the rebuttal phase. The datasets used are the ICML 2023 dataset, which is analyzed for papers that do not undergo major revisions and those that are accepted without rejection by the program committee (PC). The experiment uses the Pearson correlation coefficient (R) and Kendall's τ to measure the degree of correlation between rebuttal alignments (owner score - author score) and the author score. The results aim to show that the proposed system's reviews are better aligned with the authors' opinions, providing evidence of its effectiveness in reducing arbitrary decisions.

Experimental_Setup.name: Public Review Scores of PAPERS
Experimental_Setup.description: The purpose of this experiment is to measure the scores given to PAPERS by the proposed AAE+CGR system. The experiment involves aggregating the scores from the AAE+CGR system and analyzing the distribution of scores over different review weights and sections. The analysis includes evaluating the impact of different review weights and comparing the scores to human reviews. The results aim to demonstrate the importance and balance of different sections in the peer review process and to provide a data-driven approach to assess the quality of papers.

notes: The results are based on the Aaai 2024 dataset.
The p-values for SINGLE-LLM vs. HUMAN, H+A+O vs. HUMAN, and H+A+O vs. SINGLE-LLM are 0.151, 1, and 0.055, respectively.
The results are based on the ICML 2023 dataset.
The metrics used are Pearson Correlation (R) and Kendall's τ.

result.image: Figures 3 and 4: The distribution of AAE+CGR scores for PAPERS for different review weights and sections.
result.description: The figures show the distribution of scores given by the AAE+CGR system over different review weights and sections. The scores are aggregated to provide a clear picture of the paper's quality. The figures demonstrate that the distribution of AAE+CGR scores for PAPERS is balanced, with higher weights given to later sections. The figures also show a balance between the scores of different sections, indicating the importance of each section in the peer review process.
